doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Getting a Local 802 card through Charlie Rouse
summary: The union transfer rules, and how Rouse's agent got him a card from Max Aarons.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: he was but I never tried to introduce myself or anything. I don’t think we did that in those days. But he came up to me and asked me to work with him. I think that was after Rouse asked me to work with him. Yeah it was after, because I remember I didn’t have a local musician’s union card. And to get one you had to transfer from your home town local, put in a formal, what they called a transfer. You might have switched from your home town local to the New York local and you had a probationary period where you couldn’t work a steady job, you could only work — you could work every night, but not in the same place. You couldn’t have a steady job. You could work all kinds of individual engagements, single engagements. And I think you could work steady weekends for two nights, maybe three nights. But you couldn’t work four, five or six nights or seven nights in one place. And I put my transfer in and worked a little here and there. And now I got the job with Nellie, which meant that I went out of town, so my transfer was voided. I had to start all over again when I came back. And maybe a month and a half or so after I came back I met Charlie Rouse and he asked me to play in his group and I said I don’t have the union card, the Local 802 card. He said oh I can straighten that out. He was booked — Les Jazz Modes were booked by Joe Glaser I think, ABC Booking, and so that the agent who handled the jazz accounts just called up the union and told them well we’re sending somebody there, give him a card. And I can remember going up to Max Aarons’ office, who was I think the secretary, and Charlie Rouse told me, just meet me at the union floor, Wednesday, blah, blah, blah, and we’ll go up to Max Aarons’ office and he’ll give you a card. And we did and we walked in and Max said, “Oh well he looks like a nice boy, okay, you’re accepted.”
